A few weeks ago I shared the first stable FrameUI release and its new charts package.
Press enter or click to view image in full size

The next part of FrameUI is focused on a different problem: starting an application from individual components is still a lot of work.
Buttons, tables, selects, dialogs, and sidebars are useful on their own. But most Angular developers eventually have to combine them into the same recurring screens: user management, permissions, settings, product CRUD, inventory, orders, and audit logs.
FrameUI now includes complete application templates for those cases.
Two connected templates
The first release contains two separate Angular applications.
The Store template includes:

• an operational overview

• a product catalog

• inventory management

• orders and fulfillment

• suppliers and purchase orders
The Administration template includes:

• user management

• roles and permissions

• an audit log

• account and organization settings
The two templates share the same application context. Store operators, products, inventory permissions, supplier access, and administrative settings belong to one coherent example rather than several unrelated demo pages.
More than static screens
I did not want the templates to be screenshots recreated in HTML.
The examples are interactive and keep their changes in local state. Users can add and edit products, duplicate records, select table rows, run bulk actions, create restock plans, move users between board columns, update permissions, and inspect details in sheets and modals.
There is no backend attached. Reloading the application resets the example data.
That boundary is intentional. The templates demonstrate frontend structure, component composition, responsive behavior, and state transitions without pretending to provide authentication, persistence, or production business logic.
Built with FrameUI components
The templates use the same primitives available in the component library:

• sidebar and navigation

• tables and pagination

• inputs, input groups, selects, and comboboxes

• sheets, modals, popovers, and hover cards

• alerts, tooltips, accordions, and collapsibles

• drag and drop

• toasts

• charts
This was also a useful test of FrameUI itself. A component API can look reasonable in an isolated example but become awkward when it has to support a complete application screen.
Building the templates exposed layout, responsive, overlay, and composition issues that smaller documentation examples did not reveal.
Available as separate Angular applications
The templates are rendered interactively inside the FrameUI documentation.
Their source also lives in two standalone Angular projects:

• projects/templates/store

• projects/templates/administration
They can be run independently, inspected as complete applications, or used as starting points for another project.
They are not intended as a fixed application architecture. The goal is to provide working screens that can be reduced, reorganized, and connected to a real backend.
What should come next?
I am interested in feedback from Angular developers who build administration tools, internal products, and operational applications.
In particular:

• Are the templates complete enough to be useful?

• Is the local-state behavior helpful when evaluating them?

• Which parts would you remove before using them?

• Which complete template should be added next?

• Would you prefer more application templates or smaller reusable page sections?
